title: A Multilayer Microfluidic Platform for the Conduction of Prolonged Cell-Free Gene Expression
protocol: Place two clean silicon wafers in a preheated oven set to 250 °C.
Leave the wafers to dehydrate overnight (~16 h).
Remove one silicon wafer from the oven.
Let the wafer cool to room temperature before proceeding.
Apply 3-4 mL of 40 XT photoresist to the center of the wafer.
Spin for 20 s at 500 rpm (110 rpm/s).
Increase the spin speed to 3100 rpm (300 rpm/s) and hold here for 30 s.
Decelerate the wafer to 0 rpm with a deceleration of 200 rpm/s.
Carefully remove any edge beading using a microfiber tissue.
Soft bake using two separate hot plates set to 70 °C and 120 °C.
Allow the wafer to sit at 70 °C for 30 s.
Transfer the wafer to the 120 °C hotplate and allow it to rest here for 3.5 min.
Return the wafer to the 70 °C hotplate for another 30 s.
Remove the wafer from the hotplate and avoid sudden temperature shocks.
Allow the wafer to cool to room temperature on a stack of microfiber tissues.
Place the flow layer photomask (emulsion side down) onto the photoresist film.
Expose the wafer using a UV lamp until a total exposure of 200 mJ/cm² is achieved.
Post-exposure bake using two hot plates set to 70 °C and 105 °C.
Allow the wafer to sit at 70 °C for 20 s.
Transfer the wafer to the 105 °C hotplate and leave it here for 40 s.
Return the wafer to the 70 °C hotplate for a further 20 s.
Allow the wafer to cool to room temperature on a stack of microfiber tissues.
Develop the wafer by transferring it to a Petri dish filled with 726 MIF photoresist developer.
Submerge the entire wafer in the developer.
Rinse the wafer with demineralized water.
Use a stereo microscope to check the wafer surface for any photoresist residue.
Return the wafer to the developer if photoresist residue can be seen.
Reflow the positive photoresist by placing the wafer on a hot plate set at 110 °C for 25 min.
Silanize the wafer as described in step 1.17.
Remove the second silicon wafer from the oven and allow it to cool to room temperature before proceeding with the spin coating.
Apply 5 mL of SU8 3050 photoresist to the center of the wafer.
Spin for 20 s at 500 rpm (110 rpm/s).
Increase the spin speed to 4,000 rpm (330 rpm/s) and hold here for 42 s.
Decelerate the wafer to 0 rpm with a deceleration of 200 rpm/s.
Carefully remove any edge beading which may have occurred during the spin coating using a microfiber tissue.
Soft bake by allowing the wafer to sit at 65 °C for 30 s.
Transfer the wafer to the 95 °C hotplate and allow it to rest here for 14 min.
Return the wafer to the 65 °C hotplate for another 30 s.
Remove the wafer from the hotplate and allow it to cool to room temperature.
Measure the intensity of the UV lamp before exposure.
Determine the exposure duration required to achieve a total exposure dosage of 260 mJ/cm².
Place the photomask (emulsion side down) onto the photoresist film.
Position the wafer underneath the UV light source.
Expose the wafer using a UV lamp until a total exposure of 260 mJ/cm² is achieved.
Post-exposure bake by placing the wafer at 65 °C for 60 seconds.
Transfer the wafer to a 95 °C hotplate and leave it there for 4.5 minutes.
Return the wafer to the 65 °C hotplate for an additional 30 seconds.
Allow the wafer to cool to room temperature on a stack of microfiber tissues.
Develop the wafer by transferring it to a Petri dish filled with mrDev-600 photodeveloper.
Submerge the entire wafer in the developer and shake the dish on a benchtop shaker to accelerate development.
Rinse the wafer with isopropanol.
Use a stereo microscope to check the wafer surface for any photoresist residue.
Return the wafer to the developer if photoresist residue can be seen.
Once fully developed, hard bake the photoresist by placing the wafer on a hot plate set at 150 °C for 1 hour.
Silanize both wafers to prevent PDMS adhesion.
Pipette 2-3 droplets of silane into a small glass vial for each wafer.
Place the vial and wafers in a desiccator.
Pull vacuum for 5-10 minutes.
Seal the desiccator and leave under vacuum for 12-16 hours.
Release the vacuum from the desiccator.
Remove the silanized wafers from the desiccator.
Rinse the wafers with water.
Dry the wafers using a stream of N2.
Store the prepared wafers until needed.
Prepare two PDMS precursor solutions by combining the base and curing agents in a plastic beaker.
Stir the two components until fully mixed for the control layer using 20 g of base agent and 1 g of curing agent (20:1 ratio).
Stir the two components until fully mixed for the flow layer using 40 g of base agent and 8 g of curing agent (5:1 ratio).
Degas both solutions in a desiccator.
Pour the 5:1 ratio PDMS mixture over the flow layer wafer placed in a Petri dish.
Spin coat the control layer wafer with 20:1 ratio PDMS, pouring 5-10 mL of the PDMS onto the center of the wafer.
Run the spin protocol for the coated wafer at 500 rpm for 15 s (100rpm/s), then increase to 1450 rpm (300 rpm/s) for 45 s, and decelerate to 0 rpm (200 rpm/s).
Place the PDMS-coated wafer on a level surface in a closed Petri dish.
Let the wafer sit for 30 min.
Remove the flow layer from the desiccator and place both layers in an oven at 80 °C.
Cure both layers for 28-30 min until the PDMS is malleable enough to manipulate, remaining slightly sticky.
Using a scalpel, remove each of the four devices from the PDMS on the flow layer wafer.
Cover the feature side of the removed device with scotch tape immediately after removal.
Roughly align the flow layer blocks on the control layer by eye, placing the feature side into contact with the control layer PDMS.
Make fine adjustments to position the flow layer blocks using a stereo microscope for channel alignment.
Apply pressure between the two PDMS layers to remove air pockets.
Pour 20:1 ratio PDMS around the aligned flow layer blocks on the control layer wafer.
Place 100 g weights on each device to ensure sufficient contact during bonding.
Return the aligned devices with weights to an 80 °C oven for at least 1.5 h and no longer than 6 h.
Remove the wafer from the oven after bonding is complete.
Extract each individual device from the control layer wafer, covering the feature side of each device with scotch tape.

Punch a single hole for each of the 9 flow layer inlets, 24 control layer channel inlets, and the single flow layer outlet of each device using a camera to ensure holes are punched within the feature boundaries.
Clean a single microscope slide with isopropanol.
Dry the slides under a stream of N2.
Place the microscope slides on a hot plate set to 150 °C for 15 min.
Use oxygen plasma ashing to bond the PDMS devices to the glass slides, applying an ashing power of 50 W for 45 s.
Ensure that the feature side of the device is facing upwards when ashing.
Place the device feature side down on the glass slide, applying pressure to remove trapped gas between the surfaces.
Place the bonded devices onto a hot plate set to 110 °C for 1 h.
Weigh down the devices to improve adhesion.
Install the pneumatic control system for the control channels.
Connect the pneumatic pressure regulator to control the flow of reaction reagents within the device.
Set up a cooling system to cool the IVTT reaction solution prior to injection into the microfluidic device.
Establish a TCP connection between the fieldbus controller and the user workstation using the manufacturer’s protocol.
Compose MODBUS commands using control software provided as supplementary files.
Send MODBUS commands via the TCP connection to the controller.
Actuate the solenoid valves using the sent commands.
Expand the fieldbus controller with eight 4-channel digital output modules, one for each solenoid valve being used.
Connect the positive wire of the first solenoid valve to the first positive output port on a digital output module.
Connect the negative wire of the first solenoid valve to one of the ground ports of the same digital output module.
Repeat steps 6 and 7 systematically for subsequent solenoids, connecting each to its corresponding output port.
For the 8-valve array, connect it to output ports 1-8 on the fieldbus controller.
For the 22-valve array, connect it to output ports 9-30 on the fieldbus controller.
Connect both valve arrays to a compressed air source using 1/4” tubing.
Set the pressure of the 22-valve array to 3 bar using a pressure regulator.
Set the pressure of the 8-valve array to 1 bar using another pressure regulator.
Connect the pressure regulator to a computer using the supplied USB-connector.
Connect the pressure regulator to a compressed air source.
Attach a male Luer to 3/32” barb connector to each of the four female Luer lock output ports of the pressure regulator.
Connect a length of soft tubing (OD: 3 mm, ID: 1 mm, L: 10 cm) to the barb.
Attach a second male Luer to 3/32” barb connector to the open end of the soft tubing.
Connect this to the fluid reservoir connector ports.
Use the provided software to set the desired pressure of each outlet of the flow regulator.
Use PVC tubing (OD: 10 mm, ID: 6 mm) to connect the water-cooling system to the cold-plate water block using compression fittings.
Fill the fluid reservoir of the water-cooling system with a coolant and gently tilt the unit to displace any trapped air.
Continuously add coolant to the reservoir to ensure it remains full.
When all the gas is removed from the system, fill the reservoir to approximately 90-95% of its maximal volume.
Coil PTFE tubing (OD: 0.042”, ID: 0.022”) onto the cold face of the Peltier element and secure this with tape.
Connect one end of the PTFE tubing to the reservoirs of the flow layer pressure control system.
Ensure that the other end of the PTFE tubing protrudes no more than 1 cm from the Peltier surface.
Insert a 5 – 10 cm length of PEEK tubing (OD: 0.794 mm, ID: 0.127 mm) into the protruding end of the PTFE tubing.
Place the hot face of the Peltier element onto the cold-plate of the water block.
Apply sufficient thermal compound to the two faces.
Ensure that the tubing, Peltier element, and cooling block are in direct contact with one another at all times.
Connect the Peltier element to the temperature controller via a serial bus connector.
Securely place a thermistor on the Peltier surface and connect its output to the temperature controller.
Turn on the water cooler.
Adapt the voltage supplied to the Peltier until the temperature stabilizes at 4 °C.
Connect the Luer stub to a male Luer to 3/32” barb nylon connector.
Insert the barb of the connector into a length of polyurethane tubing (OD: 4 mm, ID: 2.5 mm).
Insert this polyurethane tubing directly into one of the solenoid valves.
Attach a 23 G, 1/2” Luer stub to a syringe and insert this into a short (3-4 cm) piece of tubing (OD: 0.06”, ID: 0.02”).
Place the open end of this tubing into a reservoir of ultrapure water.
Fill the syringe with ultrapure water.
Insert a metal pin into the open end of the tubing attached to the syringe for each control channel.
Inject water into the control channel tubing until half the length has been filled.
Disconnect the tubing from the syringe and insert the stainless-steel connector pin into the corresponding hole of the microfluidic device.
Repeat the above steps for all control channels.
Use the control interface to open all the solenoid valves.
Cut a length of tubing with OD 0.06” and ID 0.02”.
Insert one end of the tubing into the reservoir until it reaches the base.
Tighten the tubing outlet to ensure an air-tight seal is achieved.
Insert a stainless-steel connection pin (OD: 0.65 mm, ID: 0.35 mm, L: 8 mm) into the open end of the tubing.
Attach a 23 G, 1/2” Luer stub to the end of a small (1 mL) syringe.
Add a short length of tubing with OD 0.06” and ID 0.02” to the Luer stub.
Place the end of this tubing into the desired reagent solution.
Fill the syringe with the reagent.
Insert the stainless-steel connector pin into the polyurethane tubing connected to the syringe.
Fill the tubing with the reagent.
Disconnect the syringe and insert the connector pin into one of the flow layer inlet holes of the microfluidic device.
Apply pressure to each of the reservoirs using the pressure regulator software to force the reagents into the microfluidic device.
Ensure that the water cooler and Peltier element are turned on.
Set the surface temperature of the Peltier to 4 °C.
Mount the cooling setup as close to the microfluidic device as possible.
Minimize the uncooled volume between the Peltier and the device inlet.
Connect one end of the PTFE tubing to tubing connected to a fluid reservoir using a stainless-steel connector pin.
Attach a short length of tubing to a Luer stub (23 G, 1/2”).
Connect a small syringe to the Luer stub with the attached tubing.
Fill the syringe with the IVTT reaction solution or other reagent.
Connect the PEEK tubing to the syringe via the connective tubing.
Apply constant pressure to the syringe to force the reagent through the PEEK tubing and into the PTFE tubing.
Disconnect the PEEK tubing from the syringe.
Insert the PEEK tubing directly into one of the flow channel inlets of the microfluidic device.
Apply pressure via the pressure regulator software to force the cooled reagent into the microfluidic device.
Place the microfluidic device with all control and flow layer tubing attached onto the microscope stage.
Close any openings on the incubator.
Set the ambient temperature of the incubator to 29°C.
Ensure that the cooling system has been turned on and set to 4°C prior to initiating the experiment.
Ensure all flow and control channels are pressurized.
Set the pressure of control channels 1-3 to 1 bar.
Pressurize control channels 9-29 at 3 bar.
Apply a pressure between 20 and 100 mbar to fluid reservoirs using the pressure regulator software.
Close the outlet of the device by pressurizing control channel 29.
Depressurize control channels 1-3 simultaneously with control channels 15-28.
Selectively depressurize control channels of the multiplexer to allow reagents to flow into the device.
Use a microscope to monitor air removal from the microfluidic device.
Increase pressure up to 350 mbar if necessary for correct reagent loading or air bubble removal.
Ensure all reagents flow correctly without introducing air using the Flush function in control software.
Simplify fluid flow monitoring by first loading a fluorophore and observing its displacement by individual reagents.
Using the microscope, locate points of interest within each reactor.
Store coordinates of identified points for imaging during calibration and experimental processes.
Determine the fluid volume displaced from each reactor during a single inflow step by executing the calibration protocol provided in the software package.
Set the Elution Buffer Channel within the control software.
Set the Fluorophore Channel within the control software.
Set the Number of Dilution Cycles (default is 10 dilutions).
Set the Number of Inflow Steps (default is 15 steps).
Set the Number of Mixing Cycles (default is 4 cycles).
Set the Time between Mixing Cycles (default is 0 seconds).
Initiate the calibration by pressing Perform Calibration Experiment.
Mix a fluorophore into all reactors for initial imaging.
Record images of the filled reactors.
Perform dilutions by metering an eluent into each reactor based on the set number of inflow steps.
Thoroughly mix the contents after adding the eluent.
Take new images after mixing.
Repeat the dilution and imaging process for the specified number of dilution cycles.
Complete the analysis as presented by the control software upon finishing the calibration.
Set the required values for the desired experiment within the virtual control interface.
Determine and set the Refresh Fraction [%] between 15 and 40% to define reactor volume displacement per cycle.
Initiate the experimental protocol by pressing the Perform Experiment button in the control interface.
Utilize reactors 1 and 8 as controls.
House identical experiments in reactors 2 through 7.
Fill each reactor with 75% IVTT solution.
Add 25% ultrapure water to reactors serving as controls.
Add 25% linear DNA solution at a concentration of 2.5 nM to experimental reactors.
Perform dilutions every 15 minutes.
Displace 30% of the reactor volume during each dilution.
Record images at the end of each dilution cycle.
Run the analysis script ‘calibrationScript.m’ provided in the supplementary files.
Select a desired ‘.nd2’ file when prompted by the script.
Optimize image intensity using the slider to ensure clear visibility of microfluidic channel edges.
Select an area inside the reactor channel for fluorescence intensity determination.
Determine the fluorescence intensity of each reactor for each recorded image.
Display results in a simple plot for visualization.
